content: The vast majority of files in mathlib start with @[expose] public section because this replicates the behavior from before the introduction of the module system. In #33731 I create a new file with a single public definition, which is not intended to be exposed. I marked the file with @[expose] public section and the definition with @[no_expose] because I was worried that if I instead just had public section with no expose, then future contributors to this file would not realize that nothing was exposed and might forget to expose a definition. What should I do in this case?

Mathlib just hasn't caught up yet. I think this is no reason to do the opposite of Lean's default behavior. We should be forced to opt-in to exposing, rather than selectively choosing to opt-out. If you're worried about someone changing it in the future, then add a comment about it at the public section location.

I think we should change the default in Mathlib (at least for newly created files) that we only use public section and anything that wants to be exposed has to be done on a per declaration basis.
I agree with this from a software engineering standpoint, as I believe that having fewer things exposed is the right long-run choice for mathlib. I updated my PR accordingly.
I don't really understand what all these things mean so I just write expose public section as an incantation in all my PRs. Is there a simple tutorial to what they mean somewhere?

A short summary:

  • public/private decides whether a constant is visible when the file is imported.
  • expose/no_expose applies to public definitions, and decides whether the value of a definition (the part after :=) is visible when the file is imported.

public section switches the default from private to public.
@[expose] section switches the default from no_expose to expose.
instance and abbrev are already @[expose] by default.

Thank you!
To check I understand - one pattern is public and no_expose on the definition, API directly after the definition in the same file, later files can't see inside the definition, abuse defeq, etc?
And another question - what is the point of making a private import? Is it for when a file adds no new constants that appear in the statement of any theorems you want to use?

Yes exactly, the idea behind not exposing a definition is that you prove all its properties in the same file, and then other files don't have access to the defeq abuse of the definition. (To gain access to the defeq abuse anyways, you can use import all)

Private imports can help with rebuild times: say B privately imports A, and C imports B. Then if you make a change in A that doesn't affect B, then C doesn't need to be rebuilt.

You can for example privately import a tactic, or privately import a file from which you are only using theorems.
